Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] PowerShell script containing hardcoded LDAP bind with plaintext password (Tchap-leak vector)
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Mass /_matrix/media/ bulk download from tchap.gouv.fr to a single endpoint (Tchap exfil) · [LLM] High-rate Matrix client API enumeration against tchap.gouv.fr (room/user/media scraping)
Mass /_matrix/media/ bulk download from tchap.gouv.fr to a single endpoint (Tchap exfil) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the 13.5GB exfiltration vector from the June 2026 Tchap breach: a single client pulling large volumes of media via the unauthenticated /_matrix/media/r0/download/ endpoint across one or more *.tchap.gouv.fr shards. Tuned to fire when an endpoint requests media at rates or total bytes that exceed normal Tchap client behaviour. Rationale: Pivots on the article's two hard IOCs (`tchap.gouv.fr`, `matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr`) plus the attacker's own confession: 'Every file ever shared on Tchap, on any shard, is downloadable without a token. The media IDs come from the messages.' The cross-shard count is the article-specific differentiator — a normal civil servant client only talks to its own homeserver shard, so >2 distinct *.tchap.gouv.fr shards from one client is the signature of the token-less media-scrape behaviour the actor described.
ATT&CKT1530 T1213.003 T1567
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Tchap desktop client doing a full media re-sync after a profile reset or fresh install
  • Mobile Tchap client catching up large backlog after a long offline period on Wi-Fi
  • DINUM / ANSSI internal admins running migration, backup, or e-discovery tooling against Tchap
  • Power users in heavily-active public chat rooms naturally pulling many shared attachments
  • Security teams or CNIL investigators performing legitimate data-extraction during this very incident response
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tchap.exe", "element.exe", "element desktop.exe")  // suppress canonical client where bulk sync is expected; keep curl/wget/python/powershell-driven downloads
Response runbook
Step 1 — triage: pull the offending account from `InitiatingProcessAccountName`/`SrcUsername`, confirm whether they normally interact with Tchap and which shard their organisation belongs to. Pull a 30-day baseline of their Tchap traffic — flag if today's volume is >5x P95 or if they touched a shard outside their org. Step 2 — contain: notify DINUM (incident contact in the DINUM press release) so they can suspend the Tchap session token and force re-auth; block outbound to tchap.gouv.fr from the endpoint at the proxy if device compromise is suspected. Step 3 — hunt: pivot on the endpoint's process tree — what process initiated the downloads (a browser, the Tchap Electron client, curl/wget, or a custom scraper)? Look for the downloaded media being repackaged (archive creation, large zip writes) and outbound transfer to non-corporate destinations.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "tchap.gouv.fr"
| where RemoteUrl has "/_matrix/media/" and RemoteUrl has "download"
| extend Shard = tostring(parse_url(RemoteUrl).Host)
| summarize Downloads = count(),
            DistinctMedia = dcount(RemoteUrl),
            ShardsTouched = dcount(Shard),
            ShardList = make_set(Shard, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where Downloads > 100 or ShardsTouched > 2  // 100 = empirical Tchap-client baseline ceiling; >2 shards from one client is anomalous (1 user = 1 shard normally)
| order by Downloads desc
let TchapShards = dynamic(["tchap.gouv.fr", "matrix.agent.education.tchap.gouv.fr"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any (TchapShards) or DstHostname has "tchap.gouv.fr"
| where Url has "/_matrix/media/" and Url has "download"
| extend Shard = tostring(parse_url(Url).Host)
| summarize Downloads = count(),
            DistinctMedia = dcount(Url),
            ShardsTouched = dcount(Shard),
            TotalBytes = sum(HttpResponseBodyBytes),
            ShardList = make_set(Shard, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Downloads > 100 or TotalBytes > 1073741824 or ShardsTouched > 2
| order by TotalBytes desc
(source:windows.sysmon OR source:proxy) (@http.url:*tchap.gouv.fr*/_matrix/media/*download* OR @http.host:(*tchap.gouv.fr OR *.tchap.gouv.fr) @http.url_path:*/\_matrix/media/*download*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(^|\.)tchap\.gouv\.fr$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function={ queries := count() | distinctShards := count(field=DomainName, distinct=true) | firstSeen := min(@timestamp) })
| queries > 100 OR distinctShards > 2
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count as downloads, dc(Web.url) as distinct_media, sum(Web.bytes_in) as bytes_pulled, values(Web.dest) as shards from datamodel=Web where Web.dest_domain="tchap.gouv.fr" OR Web.dest="*.tchap.gouv.fr" Web.url="*/_matrix/media/*download*" by Web.src, Web.user, _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name("Web")` | where downloads > 100 OR bytes_pulled > 1073741824 OR mvcount(shards) > 2 | sort - bytes_pulled
| tstats summariesonly=false count as downloads, dc(Web.url) as distinct_media, sum(Web.bytes_in) as bytes_pulled, values(Web.dest) as shards from datamodel=Web where Web.dest_domain="tchap.gouv.fr" OR Web.dest="*.tchap.gouv.fr" Web.url="*/_matrix/media/*download*" by Web.src, Web.user, _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name("Web")` | where downloads > 100 OR bytes_pulled > 1073741824 OR mvcount(shards) > 2 | sort - bytes_pulled
PowerShell script containing hardcoded LDAP bind with plaintext password (Tchap-leak vector) AIWeaponization High
Hunts for the exact artefact class the Tchap actor harvested: PowerShell scripts that embed `New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectoryEntry` / `LDAP://` bind strings alongside plaintext password assignments. Designed for proactive discovery so credentials can be rotated before they leak via chat — and for retrospective hunting on endpoints whose users have Tchap clients installed. Rationale: Built straight from the article's credential-leak claim: 'hardcoded LDAP credentials allegedly leaked via a PowerShell script shared by a French tax authority regional director.' The dual regex — LDAP bind primitive AND a `password=` literal in the same command-line / script body — is what distinguishes a credential-bearing script from a benign AD-query script. Hunting tier because the goal is proactive discovery of these artefacts on civil-servant endpoints before they get pasted into Tchap, not real-time alerting.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1213
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admins running legitimate one-off scripts with vaulted service-account credentials (e.g., Veeam, backup tooling, scheduled AD-report jobs)
  • Legacy DSC / Group Policy scripts that embed bind credentials by design
  • Red-team or penetration-test toolkits (e.g., PowerView, Invoke-Mimikatz wrappers) running with internal authorisation
  • Compliance / audit scripts that read AD using a known service account whose password is in a secrets manager but passed inline
  • Training / demo scripts on developer workstations following Microsoft AD tutorials verbatim
Suppression filter
and not (AccountName in~ ("svc-adaudit","svc-dsc","svc-veeambackup") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("taskhostw.exe","vssvc.exe","services.exe"))  // suppress known service-account vaulted scripts run under non-interactive contexts
Response runbook
Step 1 — triage: extract the script body (cmdline or DeviceEvents AMSI dump). Confirm whether the password literal is a real, current credential or a placeholder/test value. Identify the LDAP target — is it production AD? Step 2 — contain: if a real credential is found, rotate it immediately and force a password change for the associated account. Search Tchap (or equivalent chat platforms) for the same script body or password string to determine whether it has already been shared; if yes, escalate to DINUM / chat-platform admins for log review. Step 3 — hunt: pivot on the author user — what else have they written or shared? Run the same regex across DeviceFileEvents for `.ps1` files at rest, against Git repos, and against any internal documentation / wiki / chat search APIs you can query. Track the bind account's recent authentications for signs of abuse.
// Hunt PowerShell processes whose command-line carries an LDAP bind AND a plaintext-password literal
let LdapPatterns = pack_array("DirectoryEntry", "LDAP://", "System.DirectoryServices", "ADSI", "DirectorySearcher");
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (LdapPatterns)
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(password|pwd|secret|userpassword|pass)\s*[:=]\s*[\"'][^\"'\s]{4,}"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AccountDomain,
          ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ProcessCommandLine,
          FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Cross-pivot: same script in DeviceFileEvents writes — likely the shareable .ps1 the actor exfiltrated
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName endswith ".ps1"
    | project FileTimestamp = Timestamp, DeviceName, ScriptFile = FileName, ScriptPath = FolderPath, ScriptSHA = SHA256
  ) on DeviceName
let LdapPatterns = dynamic(["DirectoryEntry", "LDAP://", "System.DirectoryServices", "ADSI", "DirectorySearcher"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any (LdapPatterns)
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(password|pwd|secret|userpassword|pass)\s*[:=]\s*[\"'][^\"'\s]{4,}"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| union (
    Event
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell" and EventID in (4103, 4104)
    | extend Script = tostring(EventData)
    | where Script has_any (LdapPatterns)
    | where Script matches regex @"(?i)(password|pwd|secret|userpassword|pass)\s*[:=]\s*[\"'][^\"'\s]{4,}"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Script
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PowerShell with hardcoded LDAP bind and plaintext password
id: 7a8e2d9c-3f1b-4c5a-b6e7-9d8f1a2b3c4e
status: experimental
description: Detects PowerShell processes whose command line contains an LDAP bind string and a plaintext password literal — the credential-exposure pattern leaked via chat in the June 2026 Tchap breach.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/french-govt-messaging-service-breached-in-account-hijacking-attack/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/09
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1552.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_image:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
  selection_ldap:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'DirectoryEntry'
      - 'LDAP://'
      - 'System.DirectoryServices'
      - 'DirectorySearcher'
  selection_pwd:
    CommandLine|re: '(?i)(password|pwd|secret|userpassword|pass)\s*[:=]\s*[\"''][^\"''\s]{4,}'
  condition: selection_image and selection_ldap and selection_pwd
falsepositives:
  - Vaulted IT-admin scripts with intentionally embedded service-account credentials
  - Penetration test / red-team kits
  - Legacy DSC configuration scripts
level: high
source:(windows.security OR windows.sysmon) @EventID:(4688 OR 1) @Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\PWSH.EXE) (@CommandLine:*DirectoryEntry* OR @CommandLine:*LDAP\://* OR @CommandLine:*System.DirectoryServices* OR @CommandLine:*ADSI*) (@CommandLine:*password=* OR @CommandLine:*Password=* OR @CommandLine:*pwd=* OR @CommandLine:*secret=*)
#event_simpleName=ScriptControlScanInfo HostName=/powershell\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)(DirectoryEntry|LDAP:\/\/|System\.DirectoryServices|DirectorySearcher|ADSI)", field=ScriptContent)
| regex("(?i)(password|pwd|secret|userpassword|pass)\s*[:=]\s*[\"\'][^\"\'\s]{4,}", field=ScriptContent)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName], function={ first := min(@timestamp) | last := max(@timestamp) | sampleScript := selectFromMin(field=@timestamp, include=[ScriptContent]) })
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count, values(Processes.process) as cmd, min(_time) as first_seen from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") (Processes.process="*DirectoryEntry*" OR Processes.process="*LDAP://*" OR Processes.process="*System.DirectoryServices*" OR Processes.process="*ADSI*") by Processes.user, Processes.dest, Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")` | where match(cmd, "(?i)(password|pwd|secret|pass)\s*[:=]\s*[\"'][^\"']{4,}") | sort - first_seen
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Processes.process) as cmd, min(_time) as first_seen from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") (Processes.process="*DirectoryEntry*" OR Processes.process="*LDAP://*" OR Processes.process="*System.DirectoryServices*" OR Processes.process="*ADSI*") by Processes.user, Processes.dest, Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")` | where match(cmd, "(?i)(password|pwd|secret|pass)\s*[:=]\s*[\"'][^\"']{4,}") | sort - first_seen
High-rate Matrix client API enumeration against tchap.gouv.fr (room/user/media scraping) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the discovery + collection behaviour the actor used to scrape ~73,000 accounts and ~650,000 messages from a single hijacked Tchap account: bursty calls to /_matrix/client/r0/sync, /joined_rooms, /publicRooms, /members from one source over a short window — orders of magnitude above what a real Matrix client does. Rationale: Anchors on the actor's quoted boast — '~650,000 messages and information on over 73,000 accounts' from one account — which is only achievable through enumeration of the Matrix client-server API. The endpoint list comes from the Matrix spec's discovery/directory routes (sync, joined_rooms, publicRooms, members, directory). Bursty per-source counts + multi-shard touch is the article-specific differentiator: the actor explicitly noted they crossed shards from a single education-shard account.
ATT&CKT1213 T1087 T1087.003
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Tchap mobile/desktop client doing initial sync after install or login on a new device (high /sync call volume)
  • Tchap Element bridge or bot account that legitimately fans out across rooms
  • DINUM/ANSSI admin tooling enumerating rooms for compliance reporting or migrations
  • Backup or e-discovery agents periodically exporting full room state
  • Load-testing or QA traffic against tchap.gouv.fr during a release window
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tchap.exe", "element.exe", "element desktop.exe", "tchap-android.apk")  // canonical client identified by process — keep curl/python/wget/headless-browser driven enumeration
Response runbook
Step 1 — triage: identify the Tchap user/session driving the requests (`SrcUsername` or Authorization-bearer-token mapping). Compare to the user's normal cadence — Matrix clients idle-poll at ~30s intervals, so 500+ calls/10min is ~25× normal. Pull the user-agent string: a real Tchap/Element client identifies itself; curl/python-requests is the actor's tooling. Step 2 — contain: notify DINUM to revoke the access token and force re-auth on that account; if a non-canonical user-agent is observed, block the source IP at the proxy. Step 3 — hunt: from the same session-IP/account, look for /_matrix/media/ bulk downloads in the same window (overlap with UC #1 above), cross-shard requests (account scoped to education shard touching matrix.agent.*.tchap.gouv.fr or other org shards), and outbound large transfers to non-corporate ASNs immediately afterwards.

New FROST Attack Lets Websites Track What Sites and Apps You Open via SSD Timing

The Hacker News
2026-06-09 7 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A malicious website can work out which sites you visit and which apps you open, using nothing but JavaScript and the timing of your SSD. The attack, called FROST, needs no native code, no extension, and no permission prompt. You open the page, leave the tab sitting there, and it watches the drive for contention in the background. Researchers at Graz University of Technology built it and

Browser writing oversized OPFS file (potential FROST SSD-timing side-channel) AIReconnaissance Low
Hunts for a browser process (Chrome/Edge/Firefox/Safari) writing a file >4 GB into the per-origin Origin Private File System storage path. FROST requires an OPFS file larger than physical RAM so reads bypass the page cache and reach the SSD — legitimate OPFS use rarely exceeds a few hundred MB, so an unexplained multi-GB OPFS allocation is the only host-side tell the Graz paper offers. Rationale: Anchored on the only host-side artefact the article actually names: 'watching your browser's storage for an unexplained multi-gigabyte file is another tell.' The >4 GB threshold mirrors FROST's stated requirement (file > physical RAM to defeat the page cache). Browser-process scope + per-origin OPFS path roots (Chrome/Edge: 'File System/' inside the profile; Firefox: 'storage/default/...fs/'; Safari/WebKit: 'Library/Safari/Storage' or 'Library/WebKit') are taken from the standardised OPFS-on-disk locations referenced by the W3C spec the article cites. No external corroboration searched — there is no actor / malware family / CVE attached, and the IOCs extracted by the pipeline (malicious.app, victim.com, receiver.app, sender.app) are clearly academic placeholders from the paper, not real C2.
ATT&CKT1592.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • In-browser IDEs (StackBlitz WebContainers, VS Code for the Web, Replit, GitPod) which legitimately allocate multi-GB OPFS sandboxes for projects
  • Web-based media editors (Photopea, Figma, CapCut Web) caching large source files
  • Browser-based games persisting asset bundles or save state to OPFS
  • Profile sync / migration tooling temporarily staging the user's browser profile inside the same directory tree
  • Service-worker caches for offline-first PWAs (e.g. mapping apps) that legitimately swell over time
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("stackblitz", "webcontainer", "vscode-web", "replit", "gitpod", "photopea", "figma", "capcut"))
// Add per-tenant: exclude origin folders for sanctioned in-browser IDEs / editors after one pass of investigation
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the origin that owns the OPFS slice (the path component immediately under '/File System/' or '/storage/default/' is the URL-encoded origin). Check the user's recent browser history / open tabs for that origin and whether it is a known-good web IDE / media editor. Pull the parent browser commandline to confirm it's an interactive session and not a headless automation harness. Step 2 — Contain: if the origin is unknown / suspicious, ask the user to close the tab (article notes the measurement only runs while the tab is open) and clear site-data for that origin in browser settings. Snapshot the OPFS file before deletion for forensic review. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the same origin across the fleet — if multiple users have a >4 GB OPFS slice from the same domain, that domain is the indicator, not the file size. Also review whether the same browser session enabled cross-origin isolation (COOP/COEP headers) by checking proxy/Zscaler/CSP-report telemetry, since FROST

title: Browser writes oversized Origin Private File System (OPFS) file - possible FROST SSD timing side-channel
id: 3f1e9a2c-1d6e-4f0a-9c4f-2b9b5e6a7c01
status: experimental
description: Detects a browser process allocating an unusually large file (>4 GB) inside its per-origin OPFS storage directory. The FROST attack (Graz Univ. of Technology, DIMVA 2026) requires an OPFS file larger than physical RAM so SSD-timing reads bypass the page cache.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-frost-attack-lets-websites-track.html
author: detection-engineering
date: 2026/06/09
tags:

  - attack.reconnaissance
logsource:

detection:

    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'

      - '\firefox.exe'

      - '/firefox'

  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:

      - '.mozilla/firefox'

  - Web-based video / photo editors caching large media (Photopea, Figma, CapCut Web)

| ContextImageFileName=/(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|Safari|WebKit)/i

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")

let LookbackDays = 7d;

Installation. Hades/Miasma PyPI poisoned package installation (26 named packages) AIDelivery High
Detects pip / python invoking installation of any of the 26 PyPI packages and versions Socket / StepSecurity identified in the Hades wave of the Miasma supply-chain campaign. Catches the very first foothold before the *-setup.pth hook runs on next interpreter start. Rationale: Uses the verbatim 26 package names from the article's two Hades clusters (the 19-package PyPI cluster + the 7-package bioinformatics cluster). Pip-install command line with these exact names is effectively zero-FP outside of incident-response activity.

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DFIR / threat-intel analyst intentionally pulling the package into a sandbox for reverse engineering
  • Internal package-mirror sync (e.g. Artifactory / Nexus PyPI proxy) caching the malicious release before takedown
  • Bioinformatics researcher pulling a legitimately-named-but-coincidental fork via an internal index URL
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !contains "sandbox" and FolderPath !has "\\malware_analysis\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot to DeviceFileEvents on the same host for any *-setup.pth file created after the install and any DeviceNetworkEvents to github.com/oven-sh/bun within 30 min — confirms full chain executed. 2) Contain: isolate host, revoke all developer secrets present (GitHub PAT, npm/PyPI tokens, AWS/GCP/Azure keys, .ssh/*, Anthropic/Claude/MCP configs), force-rotate before reconnecting. 3) Hunt: search the org for any other host that pulled the same package versions in the last 14 days; check internal package mirrors for cached copies; check GitHub org for any repo with description matching 'Hades*The End for the Damned' indicating exfil happened.

Python interpreter downloading Bun runtime ZIP from oven-sh GitHub release AIInstallation High
Hades/Miasma stages a JavaScript stealer by having the malicious .pth or __init__.py hook download the standalone Bun runtime ZIP from github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases. Detecting Python/pip as the parent of that network connection is the cleanest cross-platform pivot — Bun is not a Python dependency in any normal supply chain. Rationale: Article: 'The compromised releases shipped a *-setup.pth file that attempts to execute automatically during Python startup, download the Bun JavaScript runtime, and run an obfuscated JavaScript payload named _index.js.' StepSecurity also notes Bun is downloaded as a standalone ZIP — pivoting on python→github.com/oven-sh/bun is the staging-link signature.
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.007
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer manually running 'pip install bun-py' or any pip wrapper that legitimately fetches Bun for a project
  • CI job using a Python-based installer/bootstrap (e.g. Ansible play that installs Bun on a dev workstation)
  • Container build step where a Python entrypoint legitimately bootstraps a Bun-based JS toolchain
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bun-py","install-bun","@nestjs","bunx"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent python's command line — was the install one of the 26 Hades package names? Pull DeviceFileEvents for any .pth or _index.js write between the Python start and the Bun download. 2) Contain: kill the Bun process tree, isolate host, snapshot ~/.bun and any extracted ZIP for forensics, revoke every dev secret the user owns (GitHub PAT, npm token, PyPI token, AWS/GCP/Azure CLI creds, Anthropic/Claude API key). 3) Hunt: look across the org for any other host where python.exe was the parent of a github.com/oven-sh/bun fetch in the last 30 days; check GitHub Actions audit log for the user's PAT scopes being used from unfamiliar runners.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","pip.exe","pip3.exe","bash","sh","curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("github.com/oven-sh/bun","objects.githubusercontent.com")
   and (RemoteUrl has_any ("bun-linux","bun-windows","bun-darwin","/releases/download/") or RemoteUrl endswith ".zip")
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","pip.exe","pip3.exe")
       or FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python","python3","pip.exe","pip3.exe")
    | project DeviceId, PyTimestamp = Timestamp, PyCmd = ProcessCommandLine
) on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (PyTimestamp .. PyTimestamp + 10m)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, PyCmd
| order by Timestamp desc
let BunUrlFrag = dynamic(["github.com/oven-sh/bun","objects.githubusercontent.com"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url has_any (BunUrlFrag)
| where Url has_any ("bun-linux","bun-windows","bun-darwin","/releases/download/") or Url endswith ".zip"
| join kind=inner (
    ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","pip")
    | project DvcHostname, PyTime = TimeGenerated, PyCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine
) on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (PyTime .. PyTime + 10m)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, DstHostname, PyCmd
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hades persistence: *-setup.pth file written into Python site-packages AIInstallation High
The Hades cluster persists by dropping a `*-setup.pth` file into a site-packages directory. Python's `site` module executes any `import`/`exec` line in a `.pth` file at every interpreter start, so this file is the auto-run primitive. Detect creation of any file matching the pattern by a non-pip writer or with executable content inside. Rationale: Article: 'the use of a *-setup.pth file that's processed by Python's site module during interpreter startup, resulting in the execution of the malicious payload after installation.' The `-setup.pth` suffix in site-packages is unusual — legitimate .pth files are typically named after the package (e.g. easy-install.pth, distutils-precedence.pth), not '<pkg>-setup.pth'.
ATT&CKT1546 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom internal setup.py / build backends that author a vendor-named '*-setup.pth' (rare but possible)
  • DFIR analyst restoring a sample for reversing into an isolated venv
  • Editable-install ('pip install -e') artefact named *-setup.pth from an unusual build tool
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--editable"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the .pth contents (Defender 'Run query' / live response → small file, plain text). Genuine .pth files are single import lines; Hades .pth contains exec() / urllib code downloading Bun. 2) Contain: delete the .pth (it executes on every python start including services), isolate host, kill any running bun / _index.js processes, revoke developer secrets owned by AccountName. 3) Hunt: search every Python venv/system site-packages on the host and across the fleet for the same filename pattern; check whether the same SHA256 appears anywhere else; pivot to the parent pip install command and check whether it shows up on any other host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith "-setup.pth"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\site-packages\", "/site-packages/", @"\dist-packages\", "/dist-packages/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName endswith "-setup.pth"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\site-packages\", "/site-packages/", @"\dist-packages\", "/dist-packages/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bun runtime reading developer credential files (.npmrc / .pypirc / .ssh / .env / cloud configs) AIActions on Objectives High
The Hades JavaScript stealer (_index.js) executes inside Bun and walks the developer's home directory for credentials: .npmrc, .pypirc, .env, .aws/credentials, .config/gcloud, .azure, .docker, ~/.ssh/, ~/.config/Claude, MCP configs, Vault tokens, shell histories. Bun touching those paths is the credential_access signature. Rationale: Article enumerates the exact target set: 'secrets associated with GitHub, npm, PyPI, RubyGems, JFrog, CircleCI, Anthropic, AWS, GCP, Azure, and Kubernetes, along with Docker configurations, Vault tokens, SSH keys, shell histories, .env files, .npmrc files, .pypirc files, Claude/MCP configurations.' Bun as the reader is what makes this fire — legitimate dev tools (git, gh, aws-cli) reading these is normal; Bun reading 3+ distinct credential paths in one session is not.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Bun-based dev tool (e.g. wrangler, supabase, drizzle) that legitimately reads .env for project config
  • Bun-based deployment script that reads .aws/credentials to deploy infra
  • Engineer running 'bun test' in a repo whose test setup reads ~/.npmrc
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wrangler","supabase","drizzle","vite","next","astro") and SecretReads < 5)
Response runbook
1) Triage: list every path Bun touched in the window (group by FolderPath); a 'real' Bun app reads ~/.env in its own project dir, malware fans out to .ssh, .aws AND .npmrc AND Claude AND .docker. Read the parent process — was Python the grandparent? Was a *-setup.pth file run? 2) Contain: kill all bun processes, isolate host, mass-revoke every secret in the read set (GitHub PATs, npm/PyPI tokens, AWS access keys, GCP service-account keys, Anthropic API keys, all SSH keys), force-rotate before reissue. 3) Hunt: pivot to GitHub audit log for unfamiliar PAT use; check the user's GitHub repos for new repos whose description matches 'Hades*The End for the Damned' (the campaign exfil marker); check whether the same Bun SHA256 has run on any other host.

gh-token-monitor service install or rm -rf wiper command (Hades self-destruct) AIActions on Objectives High
Hades installs a background service named 'gh-token-monitor' that doubles as a wiper — if the developer revokes the stolen GitHub token, the service triggers `rm -rf ~/; rm -rf ~/Documents`. Either the service-install or the wiper command is article-specific and warrants an alert. Rationale: Article: 'Install a background service named gh-token-monitor that acts as a wiper by removing all data (rm -rf ~/; rm -rf ~/Documents) if the stolen GitHub token is revoked by the developer.' The service name and the exact wiper command line are both unique enough to alert directly on string match.
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1543.002 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal red-team / purple-team replicating the Hades chain in a lab
  • Security researcher detonating the malware in a controlled VM with EDR shipping to prod tenant
  • Sysadmin's deliberate cleanup script that happens to chain rm -rf ~ with rm -rf ~/Documents (highly unusual)
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is a CRITICAL — wiper attempts may already be running. Immediately check whether the rm -rf process completed and how much was destroyed (DeviceFileEvents on FileDeleted for the same DeviceId, last 5 min). 2) Contain: isolate host instantly (Defender Live Response 'isolate'), kill the gh-token-monitor service before it triggers, snapshot the disk for forensics, restore from backup if data is gone. 3) Hunt: search the whole fleet for the same service name and the same rm -rf command pattern in last 30 days; check GitHub audit log for the dev's PAT being used from unfamiliar runners (the wiper trigger is PAT revocation, so revocation may be in flight); search GitHub for any new repo by the user described 'Hades*The End for the Damned' indicating exfil completed before the wiper armed.
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "gh-token-monitor"
     and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sc create","sc.exe create","systemctl","launchctl","New-Service","systemd")
  | extend Pivot = "service_install"
),
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)rm\s+-rf\s+(~/?|/home/[^/\s]+/?|/Users/[^/\s]+/?)\s*;\s*rm\s+-rf\s+~?/?Documents"
  | extend Pivot = "wiper"
),
( DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType == "ServiceInstalled"
  | where AdditionalFields has "gh-token-monitor" or FileName has "gh-token-monitor" or ProcessCommandLine has "gh-token-monitor"
  | extend Pivot = "service_event"
)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Pivot, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
( ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "gh-token-monitor"
     and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("sc create","sc.exe create","systemctl","launchctl","New-Service")
  | extend Pivot = "service_install"
),
( ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)rm\s+-rf\s+(~/?|/home/[^/\s]+/?|/Users/[^/\s]+/?)\s*;\s*rm\s+-rf\s+~?/?Documents"
  | extend Pivot = "wiper"
),
( SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where EventID == 7045
  | where ServiceName has "gh-token-monitor" or ServiceFileName has "gh-token-monitor"
  | extend Pivot = "service_event", ActingProcessCommandLine = ServiceFileName, DvcHostname = Computer, ActorUsername = SubjectUserName
)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, Pivot, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Hades Wiper Command or gh-token-monitor Service Install
id: 7c5b9e8a-2d3c-4f5b-9e7d-3a4b5c6d7e8a
description: Detects either installation of a service literally named 'gh-token-monitor' or execution of the Hades wiper command 'rm -rf ~/; rm -rf ~/Documents' attributed to the Hades / Miasma PyPI campaign.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/hades-pypi-attack-19-packages-poisoned.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/09
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.impact
  - attack.t1543.003
  - attack.t1485
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_service:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'gh-token-monitor'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'sc create'
      - 'sc.exe create'
      - 'systemctl'
      - 'launchctl'
      - 'New-Service'
  selection_wiper:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'rm -rf'
      - 'Documents'
    CommandLine|re: '(?i)rm\s+-rf\s+(~|/home/|/Users/).*;\s*rm\s+-rf\s+~?/?Documents'
  condition: selection_service or selection_wiper
level: critical

(source:windows.sysmon OR source:windows.security OR source:linux.auditd) AND ((@CommandLine:(*gh-token-monitor*) AND @CommandLine:(*sc?create* OR *systemctl* OR *launchctl* OR *New-Service*)) OR (@process.command_line:(*gh-token-monitor*) AND @process.command_line:(*systemctl* OR *launchctl* OR *sc?create*)) OR @CommandLine:("rm -rf ~/*; rm -rf ~/Documents" OR "rm -rf ~; rm -rf ~/Documents") OR @process.command_line:("rm -rf ~/*; rm -rf ~/Documents" OR "rm -rf ~; rm -rf ~/Documents"))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (CommandLine=/gh-token-monitor/i AND CommandLine=/(sc\s+create|systemctl|launchctl|New-Service)/i) OR CommandLine=/rm\s+-rf\s+(~\/?|\/home\/[^\/\s]+|\/Users\/[^\/\s]+)\s*;\s*rm\s+-rf\s+~?\/?Documents/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
(`endpoint_processes` OR `linux_processes`)
| eval is_service_install=if(match(process,"(?i)gh-token-monitor") AND (match(process,"(?i)(sc\\.exe|sc\\s+create|systemctl|launchctl|new-service)")),1,0),
       is_wiper=if(match(process,"(?i)rm\\s+-rf\\s+(~/?|/Users/[^/]+|/home/[^/]+)\\s*;\\s*rm\\s+-rf\\s+~?/Documents") OR match(process,"(?i)rm\\s+-rf\\s+~/?\\s*;?\\s*rm\\s+-rf\\s+~/Documents"),1,0)
| where is_service_install=1 OR is_wiper=1
| stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(process) as commands by host user parent_process_name process_name is_service_install is_wiper
Hades C2: GitHub commit search for campaign markers TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime / firedalazer AICommand & Control High
Hades retrieves staged payloads by polling the GitHub commits API for two unique marker strings: 'TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime' (Base64 JS payload) and 'firedalazer' (Python dropper). Either string appearing in process command lines, HTTP requests, or DNS/URL telemetry on a dev host is a high-fidelity C2 indicator. Rationale: Article: 'the malware queries GitHub commits for the keyword TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime to extract a Base64-encoded string containing a JavaScript payload. It also polls GitHub for commits matching the keyword firedalazer so as to fetch a Python-based dropper.' Both strings are sufficiently unique (random-looking concatenations) that any appearance in process/web/DNS telemetry is essentially zero-FP outside of threat-hunting activity.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst pasting the IOC into a curl / gh CLI command for verification
  • Security tool (EDR, SOAR) running a containment query that includes the marker string
  • Internal blog/wiki page mentioning the IOC being fetched into a browser (unlikely on hash/URL telemetry, but possible in proxy logs)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gh.exe","gh","curl.exe","curl") or AccountName !in~ ("soc-analyst","threat-intel")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which process/host issued the query — if it's a security analyst's gh CLI or a SOAR enrichment query, dismiss. If it's bun / python / a previously-unknown binary, treat as live C2. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the calling process tree, snapshot any retrieved payload from disk (look for base64 blobs / .py / .js dropped in the last hour), revoke every developer secret on the host. 3) Hunt: pivot fleet-wide for the same two strings in process and web telemetry over the last 60 days; check whether any host queried github.com/oven-sh/bun in the same window (would chain to UC 2); search GitHub commits for the same marker strings in the org's own repos.
let Markers = dynamic(["TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (Markers)
  | extend Pivot = "process", Url = ""
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Pivot, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, Url
),
( DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteUrl has_any (Markers)
  | extend Pivot = "network", FileName = InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Pivot, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, Url = RemoteUrl
)
| order by Timestamp desc
let Markers = dynamic(["TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime","firedalazer"]);
union isfuzzy=true
( ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (Markers)
  | extend Pivot = "process", Url = ""
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, Pivot, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Url
),
( ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Url has_any (Markers)
  | extend Pivot = "web", ActingProcessName = "", ActingProcessCommandLine = "", ActorUsername = SrcUsername
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname = SrcHostname, ActorUsername, Pivot, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Url
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Hades Campaign GitHub C2 Marker Strings
id: 5a6b7c8d-9e0f-1a2b-3c4d-5e6f7a8b9c0d
description: Detects either of the two Hades / Miasma GitHub commit-marker strings (TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime, firedalazer) appearing in a process command line — the malware searches GitHub for these to retrieve Base64-encoded JS payload and the Python dropper respectively.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/hades-pypi-attack-19-packages-poisoned.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/09
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1102.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime'
      - 'firedalazer'
  condition: selection
level: high

(@CommandLine:(*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime* OR *firedalazer*) OR @process.command_line:(*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime* OR *firedalazer*) OR @http.url:(*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime* OR *firedalazer*) OR @http.url_details.queryString:(*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime* OR *firedalazer*) OR @DestinationHostname:(*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime* OR *firedalazer*))
(#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/(TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime|firedalazer)/i) OR (#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime|firedalazer)/i) OR (#event_simpleName=ScriptControlScanInfo ScriptContent=/(TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime|firedalazer)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, #event_simpleName], function=count())
NETWORK
(`endpoint_processes` Processes.process IN ("*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime*","*firedalazer*"))
| eval pivot="process"
| append [ search `web_logs` (url="*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime*" OR url="*firedalazer*" OR uri_query="*TheBeautifulSnadsOfTime*" OR uri_query="*firedalazer*") | eval pivot="web" ]
| stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(process) as commands values(url) as urls by host user pivot
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c") or SHA1 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c") or MD5 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c") or SHA1 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c") or MD5 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process_hash
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.file_hash IN ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c")

Check Point VPN IKEv1 authenticated session without machine certificate (CVE-2026-50751) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the exploitation primitive for CVE-2026-50751: Remote Access VPN / Mobile Access / Spark gateway sessions negotiated via the deprecated IKEv1 key exchange, on gateways not enforcing machine-certificate authentication. Surfaces the vulnerable configuration state being actively used and any successful IKEv1 logins from the article's external IPs. Rationale: Targets the exact preconditions named in the Check Point advisory: IKEv1 + no machine cert + legacy Remote Access clients. Anchors on the 8 article-confirmed source IPs to keep FPs near zero. Cross-checked against the CISA KEV listing for CVE-2026-50751 and Check Point's published mitigation guidance (IKEv2-only + mandatory Machine Certificate Authentication). Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://support.checkpoint.com/results/sk/sk183001
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Authentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users on legacy SecuRemote/SecureClient endpoints that haven't been migrated to IKEv2 yet
  • Penetration testing or red-team exercises authorized against the VPN appliance
  • Vendor support engineer connecting from a partner range that happens to overlap a flagged ASN
  • Backup VPN concentrator in a lab still running pre-patch firmware for regression testing
Suppression filter
| where SourceUserName !endswith "-svc" and SourceUserName !in~ ("backup-account","vendor-support") and not (DeviceCustomString1 has "TestLab" or Message has "penetration-test")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP in CommonSecurityLog matches the article's Qilin set; pull the AccountName/SourceUserName and check whether the user is still using legacy SecuRemote and whether MFA was satisfied. Pivot to SigninLogs and DeviceLogonEvents for the same user in the next 6h. 2) Contain: terminate the active VPN session on the gateway, disable the user account, force-rotate the user's domain password, and block the source IP at the perimeter; if patch is not yet applied, enforce the Check Point mitigation (IKEv2-only + mandatory Machine Certificate Authentication) immediately. 3) Hunt: search 30 days of CommonSecurityLog for any prior IKEv1 success from external IPs, and pivot every internal host that received traffic from a VPN-assigned client IP for early Qilin TTPs (vssadmin shadow delete, BCDedit, esxcli vm kill, .qilin extension drops).
// Defender does not natively ingest Check Point gateway logs; this pivots on inbound VPN egress traffic observed by onboarded endpoints to Qilin IPs that just authenticated via the Check Point appliance.
let QilinIPs = dynamic(["45.77.149.152","209.182.225.136","38.60.157.139","162.33.177.101","45.76.26.42","144.208.127.155","38.54.88.201","38.54.107.167"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (QilinIPs) or LocalIP in (QilinIPs)
| where RemotePort in (500, 4500, 443)  // IKE / IKE-NAT-T / SSL-VPN
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP, LocalPort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let QilinIPs = dynamic(["45.77.149.152","209.182.225.136","38.60.157.139","162.33.177.101","45.76.26.42","144.208.127.155","38.54.88.201","38.54.107.167"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Check Point"
| where DeviceProduct in~ ("VPN-1 & FireWall-1","Mobile Access","Quantum Spark","SmartDefense","Security Gateway")
| where (Message has_any ("IKEv1","IKE_v1","Phase 1","Legacy Remote Access","SecuRemote") 
         or DeviceCustomString1 has_any ("IKEv1","Legacy Remote Access")
         or DeviceCustomString2 has_any ("IKEv1","Legacy Remote Access"))
| where DeviceAction in~ ("accept","Key Install","Log") or EventOutcome =~ "success"
| where SourceIP in (QilinIPs) or Message has_any (QilinIPs)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, SourceUserName, DeviceAction, Activity, Message, DeviceCustomString1, DeviceCustomString2
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound EDR traffic to Check Point CVE-2026-50751 / Qilin affiliate infrastructure AICommand & Control High
Hunts any endpoint reaching out to the 8 IP indicators tied to Qilin affiliate exploitation of CVE-2026-50751 — catches both inbound exploit attempts replayed in flow telemetry and post-compromise C2/staging beacons from VPN-assigned internal hosts. Rationale: Eight article-confirmed IPs make this a clean IOC-pivot. Network-only detection avoids dependence on the Check Point appliance forwarding its logs. CloudWatch query left empty — Qilin C2 lives on Windows endpoints, not CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platform validation traffic (e.g. analyst sandbox curl-ing the IP)
  • Recycled IPs being reassigned to legitimate SaaS after the campaign window closes
  • Honeypot/canary deployments deliberately reaching out to known-bad infrastructure
  • Security awareness training tools simulating malicious destinations
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\TI-Sandbox\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot the DeviceName from DeviceNetworkEvents into DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceLogonEvents for the same hour — was this a VPN-assigned client IP (10.x range from the Check Point pool) and was there a fresh interactive logon? 2) Contain: isolate the device via Defender live-response or Falcon network-contain, kill the initiating process, and block all 8 IPs at the perimeter and EDR firewall. 3) Hunt: across all endpoints, hunt for the two article MD5s (52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689, 51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce), suspicious vssadmin/bcdedit usage on hosts that received traffic from the VPN pool, and any new local admin accounts created within 2h of the connection.
let QilinIPs = dynamic(["45.77.149.152","209.182.225.136","38.60.157.139","162.33.177.101","45.76.26.42","144.208.127.155","38.54.88.201","38.54.107.167"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(45d)
| where RemoteIP in (QilinIPs)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort), Procs=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName)
  by DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by FirstSeen asc
let QilinIPs = dynamic(["45.77.149.152","209.182.225.136","38.60.157.139","162.33.177.101","45.76.26.42","144.208.127.155","38.54.88.201","38.54.107.167"]);
union isfuzzy=true
( CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(45d)
  | where DestinationIP in (QilinIPs) or SourceIP in (QilinIPs)
  | project TimeGenerated, Vendor=DeviceVendor, Product=DeviceProduct, Src=SourceIP, Dst=DestinationIP, DstPort=DestinationPort, User=SourceUserName, Action=DeviceAction, Bytes=ReceivedBytes ),
( ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(45d)
  | where DstIpAddr in (QilinIPs) or SrcIpAddr in (QilinIPs)
  | project TimeGenerated, Vendor=EventVendor, Product=EventProduct, Src=SrcIpAddr, Dst=DstIpAddr, DstPort=DstPortNumber, User=SrcUsername, Action=DvcAction, Bytes=NetworkBytes )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Qilin affiliate payload hash execution / write (CVE-2026-50751 post-compromise) AIInstallation High
Hunts for execution or file-write of the two MD5 hashes Check Point/CISA attributed to Qilin affiliate activity following CVE-2026-50751 VPN exploitation. High-fidelity IOC match across process, image-load, and file-write telemetry. Rationale: MD5s come directly from the article's IOC bundle and triangulate against the Qilin affiliate attribution Check Point published. Hash IOCs across process/file/image-load tables cover both staging and live execution paths. CloudWatch left empty — these are endpoint binaries, not CloudTrail-shaped. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1032/
ATT&CKT1486 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AV/EDR vendor sample submissions that record the hash in test telemetry
  • Malware analysis VM where an analyst intentionally detonated the sample
  • Threat-intel feed integration that writes the hash into a local lookup file on a SIEM host
  • False positive on collision (vanishingly unlikely for MD5 in this context)
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\ProgramData\Malware-Samples\" and FolderPath !contains "FlareVM" and DeviceName !startswith "MAL-VM-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hash on a single host is the binary itself (not a TI feed file path). Pull ProcessCommandLine, ParentImage, and the user under which it ran; pivot 6h backward to find the delivery vector (was it a fresh VPN logon from a flagged IP?). 2) Contain: network-isolate the host immediately, snapshot disk for forensics, kill the process tree, force-rotate credentials for all users who logged into the host in the last 14d, and submit the hash to your EDR's blocklist. 3) Hunt: across the fleet, search for the 8 Qilin IPs in DeviceNetworkEvents, vssadmin/wmic shadow copy deletions in DeviceProcessEvents, .qilin extension drops in DeviceFileEvents, and any successful Check Point IKEv1 logon in the last 30d in CommonSecurityLog.
let QilinHashes = dynamic(["52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689","51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce"]);
union isfuzzy=true
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(45d)
  | where MD5 in (QilinHashes) or InitiatingProcessMD5 in (QilinHashes)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType="ProcessExec", FileName, FolderPath, MD5, ProcessCommandLine, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine ),
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(45d)
  | where MD5 in (QilinHashes)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType=tostring(ActionType), FileName, FolderPath, MD5, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine ),
( DeviceImageLoadEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(45d)
  | where MD5 in (QilinHashes)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType="ImageLoad", FileName, FolderPath, MD5, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine )
| order by Timestamp desc
let QilinHashes = dynamic(["52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689","51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce"]);
union isfuzzy=true
( SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(45d)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where FileHash has_any (QilinHashes)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Account, FileHash ),
( ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(45d)
  | where MD5 in (QilinHashes) or Hash in (QilinHashes)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, NewProcessName=TargetProcessName, CommandLine=TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, Account=ActorUsername, FileHash=MD5 ),
( ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(45d)
  | where TargetFileMD5 in (QilinHashes) or Hash in (QilinHashes)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, NewProcessName=ActingProcessName, CommandLine=ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName="", Account=ActorUsername, FileHash=TargetFileMD5 )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.defender OR windows.security) (@Hashes:(*52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689* OR *51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce*) OR @MD5:(52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689 OR 51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce) OR @FileHash:(52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689 OR 51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce))
